Python 3; Lesson 2 additionally uses the existing pygame/pygame-teaching-pack.zip and its pinned requirements. Read the unit3-fluency chapter and foundations workbook. Use fictional values and disposable history files only. No extra assessment or homework. Suggested 55-minute plans are untrialled; select one repair rather than completing every extension.

slides.title: Python diagnosis and targeted repair
body: Unit 3 · Week 1 · Lesson 1
Trace first, then choose one skill to repair.
slides.notes: 2027 teaching edition; retrieval of Year 11 prerequisites, not a new assessment. Keep diagnostic responses separate from later corrections. All resources and keys are public; record prior exposure.

slides.title: An independent starting point
body: Predict the result for [3, 5, 8] and [].
Explain the boundary and one possible fault.
slides.notes: Use workbook D1–D4 without running code or opening the key. D1 uses this code; D2 checks a returned result, D3 classifies three faults, D4 selects boundary/empty tests. Record unaided, supported or previously seen. Stop and preserve responses before the next slide. Do not infer a grade from this short sample.

slides.title: Feedback after the diagnostic
body: The counts are 2 and 0.
The value 5 belongs in the count.
Keep corrections beside the original responses.
slides.notes: Only reveal after original work is preserved. D2 returns 2 while caller count remains 10. D3 missing colon: SyntaxError; int("two"): ValueError at runtime; >5 in an inclusive rule: logic fault. An empty list does not execute the loop. Ask students to explain a mismatch before giving the next step; use teacher key D1–D4.

slides.title: A count changes at the condition
body: Trace the running count after each value.
Explain why initialisation is outside the loop.
slides.notes: Trace [4,5,7]: start0; after4=0, after5=1, after7=2. Hide the final row until students predict it. Resetting count inside the loop loses earlier matches. Connect to the allocated exit check. Use a paper trace if Python is unavailable.

slides.title: One repair, with less support
body: Choose boundary, return value or error diagnosis.
Predict, run, explain, then change one input.
A partner asks for reasons before offering a fix.
slides.notes: Use workbook R1/R2/R3; choose the weakest diagnostic item, not all three. R1 remove the suggested predicate; R2 repair a missing return; R3 isolate a runtime conversion from a logic comparison. Retain expected/actual and smallest failing example. Secure students may compare local rebinding with list mutation using foundations workbook D; this is optional.

slides.title: A changed unaided check
body: Count values >= 6 in [6, 2, 9, 6].
Also predict the empty-list result.
Close the worked trace and explain your rule.
slides.notes: Fresh values and threshold: expected3 and0. Ask students to write or trace a function without the model; record any help. An immediate retry is formative evidence, not proof of lasting mastery. If boundary fails, compare >= and > using exactly6 before another changed retry.

slides.title: Evidence for the next repair
body: Compare original, correction and changed retry.
Name the first incorrect step and its cause.
slides.notes: Use workbook record: item, expected, actual, explanation, help, next step. Avoid only writing careless mistake. Group students for Lesson2 by observed needs. A student with no previous Pygame experience starts with stage1 and teacher modelling; do not assume prior use.

slides.title: Exit: count and empty input
body: Trace values >= 5 in [4, 5, 7], then [].
Explain where the counter is initialised.
slides.notes: Allocated check u3-l1:2 and0; initialise before iteration; include exact boundary. Collect an unaided explanation. Revisit a changed count during later retrieval within existing lessons; no added homework.

slides.title: Pygame re-entry and one focused repair
body: Unit 3 · Week 1 · Lesson 2
Retrieve Python skills through the existing lab.
Record experience; choose one repair target.
slides.notes: Use existing y12-1 bridge: stages1–4 are a rapid re-entry menu, not four full labs to finish today. Match the existing 5/10/15/15/5/5 phase budget. Ask about prior Pygame use. Newcomers start with stage1; secure learners inspect function/list/history evidence. Use paper tracing provisionally if install fails, then schedule actual execution in existing support time.

slides.title: One frame, in the supplied runner
body: Run stage1_loop.py, then lab_runner.py 2.
Trace events, held keys, update and draw.
Predict before moving or pausing the player.
slides.notes: Extract the existing Pygame pack together in a writable folder. Install its requirements using school-approved procedures. Stage1 is the smallest window/movement loop. Stage2 connects new_state(), command() and update(). The supplied dictionary is infrastructure; do not start classes or the Year12 project. Events are discrete messages; held-key state is sampled after processing events. X/Escape quit. Sources: https://www.pygame.org/docs/ref/event.html and https://www.pygame.org/docs/ref/time.html

slides.title: Milliseconds become movement
body: Predict the displacement before running.
200 pixels/second × 250 ms / 1000 = 50 pixels.
slides.notes: Use lab_rules.SPEED=200. Fresh worked state starts x308, ready, remaining20000. command(state,"space") then update(state,1,250,collect=False) gives x358 and19750ms. This direct rule call is a test after the start transition, not the runner transition frame. Compare with the runner, which discards elapsed time on start/pause/resume/reset frames. Do not confuse pixels/frame with pixels/second.
slides.code:
displacement = direction * SPEED * dt_ms / 1000
# direction=1, SPEED=200, dt_ms=250
# displacement=50 pixels

slides.title: Pairs explain a fault before editing
body: Syntax: a missing colon.
Runtime: int("two").
Logic: using milliseconds as seconds.
slides.notes: Use copies or the workbook snippets; leave the known-good lab untouched. Predictor names expected behaviour; driver reproduces and changes one cause, then swap. Missing colon prevents parsing; ValueError occurs when conversion executes; removing /1000 gives wrong displacement without necessarily raising an exception. Some wrong units may clamp x at the boundary and hide the original error. Inspect raw displacement as well as screen output.

slides.title: A small rule with faded support
body: In a copy, complete movement/time in update().
Use direction 1, 250 ms and collect=False.
Preserve bounds, timeout and paused behaviour.
slides.notes: Use faded_practice.py:160pixels/second, x40, remaining15000. Complete only the teacher-selected movement/time branch, not every TODO. Set a fresh state to playing for the rule test. With collect=False expect x80,14750ms. Validate direction/dt and return unchanged unless playing. Timeout before movement/collection; bound0..616. The full graphical runner still has worked two-station display assumptions: do not claim the changed three-station game is integrated. Newcomers can complete the smaller worksheet predicate with teacher support then take a changed unaided trace.

slides.title: A fresh explanation without the model
body: Predict 500 ms movement at 160 pixels/second.
Explain paused time and reset after a long gap.
slides.notes: Hide the worked calculation and close the key. New fresh state, playing,collect=False: x120 and14500ms;80pixels displacement. For paused calls update returns unchanged; runner pause/resume/reset events discard that frame delta. R creates ready state, x308 in worked lab or40 in faded, fresh active flags and full duration. Teacher checks one changed case rather than assigning all stages.

slides.title: Targeted list or file inspection
body: Choose one: collect-once flags or valid history.
Predict, run and record expected versus actual.
slides.notes: Use stage3/4 only as the selected repair. Stage3: repeated contact with inactive station adds no score; do not remove entries during traversal. Stage4: temporary history 0,2,bad,3 accepts0/2 and warns twice; missing/empty valid. Save only after finished, append once, mark saved after success. Use disposable paths. If time is needed for beginner repair, keep this as teacher demonstration and record follow-up rather than inventing extra time.

slides.title: Exit: events, held keys and elapsed time
body: Explain a key event versus held-key state.
Verify pause/reset after a long elapsed interval.
slides.notes: Allocated u3-l2 check. Demonstrate actual run where available and record exact case in practice-tests.csv/readiness.csv. Paused gameplay unchanged; reset fresh under lab rules; transition frame ignored. If frames are treated as seconds, trace dt_ms explicitly. This is a diagnostic bridge, not evidence that the whole project is ready.

slides.title: Requirement changes and regression tests
body: Unit 3 · Week 1 · Lesson 3
Revise a rule and justify the tests to rerun.
slides.notes: Retain existing lesson scope: linear/iterative comparison, requirement change and transfer test. Consolidate syntax/runtime/logic diagnosis while revising a small Python rule. No new assessment or project features.

slides.title: Retrieval: three kinds of fault
body: Classify a missing colon and int("two").
A rule uses > 5 when the boundary is inclusive.
Give evidence for each classification.
slides.notes: Ask for predictions first. SyntaxError at parsing; ValueError when executed; logic fault produces wrong result. Use fresh small examples if these have already been seen. Students identify stage, cause and minimal failing input; avoid equating all exceptions with syntax errors.

slides.title: Two ways to organise development
body: Linear: plan successive stages and their hand-offs.
Iterative: build, test, review and revise a version.
Both need requirements, records and testing.
slides.notes: Explain investigate/analyse/design/develop/implement/evaluate in the chapter’s terms. A linear process can authorise a documented return when requirements change; it is not incapable of change. Iteration still needs a plan and acceptance criteria. Ask pairs which approach suits stable versus evolving rules, and what the cost of rework is. Do not claim one process is universally best.

slides.title: The changed requirement is precise
body: Old rule: count values >= 5.
New rule: count values >= 6.
For [5, 6, 7], predict the new count.
slides.notes: Record change C01,reason,boundary and affected predicate. Old expected3; new expected2. Update requirement/design/implementation/test expectations together. Show the parameterised function in the workbook after predictions. A syntax fault, runtime conversion or wrong > predicate needs different evidence, not random edits.

slides.title: Guided repair and regression
body: Test below, at and above the new threshold.
Retest empty and duplicate values.
Record expected, actual and version.
slides.notes: Use workbook C01. For threshold6: [5]=0,[6]=1,[7]=1,[]=0,[6,6]=2. Recheck threshold5 call [4,5,7]=2 in parameterised function: previously valid behaviour remains supported. If restoring old logic simply to pass old expectations, distinguish changed requirements from regression. Teacher models one test then fades the remaining expected column.

slides.title: A fresh requirement, independently
body: Change the minimum to 8.
Write tests before changing or running the code.
Explain one retained regression case.
slides.notes: Close model. [7,8,9,8]=>3,[]=0,[8,8]=>2. Write count_at_least(values,minimum), then run checks, record help and retain original attempt. Optional secure-learner extension: specify a policy for nonnumeric input and justify where validation belongs; do not silently add it to common requirements.

slides.title: Peer moderation of the explanation
body: Check the boundary, not just the final total.
Explain how the chosen process handles C01.
slides.notes: Use key only after preserving the independent solution. Partner asks which evidence establishes the boundary and which case protects unchanged behaviour. Explain iterative revisit of design/build/test and controlled linear return with updated documents. A passing sample is not proof of absence of faults.

slides.title: Exit: a client changes the threshold
body: Compare linear and iterative responses.
Give a regression case and its expected result.
slides.notes: Allocated u3-l3. Expected: iteration revisits design/build/test; linear may need a controlled return; retest previously valid behaviour. If iterative is described as no planning, ask for documented revision and acceptance criteria. Record an unresolved fault for later retrieval.

slides.title: Versions, restoration and retesting
body: Unit 3 · Week 1 · Lesson 4
Restore an earlier version without losing current work.
slides.notes: Use companion version exercise; all files are small fictional counter examples. This is hands-on recovery evidence, not a claim that a filename alone proves a backup. No Git account needed.

slides.title: Retrieval: what is recovery evidence?
body: A filename says v1. Does that prove restoration?
What would you run and record to check?
slides.notes: Elicit contents/location/version/test evidence. A copied filename or screenshot alone cannot establish that runnable earlier code was restored. Discuss separate destination and preserving working-v2 before the model.

slides.title: A known baseline and a changed working copy
body: Run seed-v1/check.py before saving a snapshot.
Copy seed-v1 to snapshot-v1 and working-v2.
Change only the working copy to minimum 6.
slides.notes: Extract pack. seed-v1 contains rules.py,check.py,VERSION.txt. Run from that folder: python check.py prints source path,version1,expected2,actual2,PASS for[4,5,7]. Copy all three files to separate folders; leave snapshot-v1 unchanged. In working-v2 set MINIMUM=6,VERSION=2, expected=1 in check.py and VERSION.txt to2 with reason. Run current v2: expected1,actual1. Use school-approved file manager or shell; no destructive commands.

slides.title: A usable version record
body: Record version, purpose, paths and test result.
Keep planned and actual changes distinct.
Retain the unchanged snapshot of version 1.
slides.notes: Use version-log.csv. Record actual date/time,changed files,why,expected/actual,working/snapshot path. A filename v1 with edited contents is not the preserved v1. Teacher models one honest record; never supply fabricated classroom results. Optional hash or version control can supplement, not replace, actual restore/run evidence.

slides.title: Restore to a separate folder
body: Copy snapshot-v1 into a new restored-v1 folder.
Run restored-v1/check.py from that folder.
Confirm the source path and version used.
slides.notes: Close model. Students perform actual restoration, not a written plan. Do not overwrite working-v2. Restored v1 should report VERSION1,MINIMUM5,expected2,actual2,PASS. Check printed rules.__file__ points to restored-v1. If it points elsewhere investigate working directory/import path. If no computer available, plan on paper and mark actual restoration pending; it needs a later device check in existing support time.

slides.title: Retest the preserved current version
body: Run working-v2/check.py again.
Explain why v1 gives 2 while v2 gives 1.
Check that current files remain intact.
slides.notes: Currentv2 threshold6 counts only7 from[4,5,7],so1; restoredv1threshold5 counts5and7,so2. A discrepancy must be investigated; do not edit the restored baseline to force a pass. Verify empty input0 for both and threshold boundary5(v1)/6(v2). Record separateactualresults and paths.

slides.title: A partner checks the evidence
body: Show the restored folder and actual test output.
Show the separate current version still working.
Identify one limit of this recovery test.
slides.notes: Partner checks log against files/run evidence,not just filename. This verifies the small example,not backup of an entire device or project. Optional extension: copy a snapshot to an approved separate storage location and retest; avoid assuming same-disk copies protect against drive failure. No mandatory cloud account.

slides.title: Exit: restore, run and identify
body: Show the separately restored version.
Rerun a known test and identify its source path.
slides.notes: Allocated u3-l4: actual restoration and expected/reasoned result recorded; filename alone is insufficient. If working files overwritten, repeat safely into a separate destination with original preserved. Explain how documented versions support controlled returns in linear work and iterations. Use remaining issues to choose next retrieval.
